case_info.scenario: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 29 weeks’ gestation, underwent amniocentesis due to a suspected polycystic kidney detected on routine fetal ultrasonography. While no genetic abnormality associated with polycystic kidney was identified (whole-exome sequencing Invitae), an incidental finding of a heterozygous c.501-2 A<G sequence variant (SV) in theRB1gene was noted. This specificRB1SV had not been previously reported in any genetic databases, but was deemed pathogenic by Invitae, the commercial laboratory, in line with the American College of Medical Genetics and their guidelines for interpretation of sequence variants.1No intraocular tumors were found on fetal sonography. There was no discernable family history of retinoblastoma or ocular disorders, and complete ophthalmic evaluation of both parents was normal with no suspected retinomas.

options.C: Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents

case_info.answer: Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents
case_info.explanation: RB1pathogenic sequence variant in a 29-week-old fetus with no family history or sonographic features suggestive of retinoblastoma. C. Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents Retinoblastoma, with an incidence of 1 in 17 000 live births, is typically diagnosed within a few years of life.2Early treatment can lead to nearly 100% survival rate. Prognosis is poor with delayed diagnosis or treatment.2Inherited retinoblastoma occurs at a younger age than sporadic disease, tends to be bilateral,3and results from biallelic pathogenic SVs (PSVs) in theRB1gene in a precursor retinal cell.4,5An inherited mutated allele (ie, germline PSV) predisposes to tumorigenesis in utero or after birth in 40% of retinoblastoma cases, with high penetrance of the disease.3,5,6 Current evidence suggests screening at-risk newborns (ie, those with a family history of retinoblastoma) until 4 years of age.7Prenatal molecular screening facilitates earlier detection, potentially improving family planning, genetic counseling, and earlier interventions.4,8For example, planned delivery for prenatally confirmed carriers ofRB1mutations can lead to earlier diagnosis, reduced treatment-associated morbidity, and favorable visual outcomes.4However, early fetal delivery has potential risks, including physical and neurocognitive delay, warranting cautious evaluation by multidisciplinary teams.4,8Furthermore, while no threshold exists for planned early delivery, premature delivery may be achieved effectively with active intervention following 26 weeks’ gestation.9 InactivatingRB1germline PSVs have been associated with high penetrance, with most PSV carriers developing intraocular tumors by early childhood. However, phenotypic presentation may differ among individuals, even among identical PSV carriers.3,6Alekseeva et al6reported a substantial prevalence of asymptomatic mutatedRB1PSV carriers among parents of retinoblastoma patients with more children inheriting a defectiveRB1gene from the father, suggesting parental origin may affect retinoblastoma penetrance. In another study, individuals harboring low-penetranceRB1PSVs (eg, splice-site and missense SVs) developed bilateral retinoblastoma later than patients with null PSVs.4Molecular screening methods (eg, RNA sequencing of amniotic fluid cells) have enabled clinicians to assess whether a specificRB1SV is likely to be associated with any phenotypic manifestations.10However, there currently are no clinically acceptable predictive parameters to better define the phenotypic expression ofRB1PSV carriers. The case presented herein reports an incidentalRB1PSV detected on unrelated genetic testing, posing a clinical and ethical dilemma to both clinician and family.3,4,6,8 Both parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (choice C), confirming the father, with no history of cancer, harbored the same genetic SV as the fetus, decreasing the possibility that the SV was pathogenic. RNA sequencing demonstrated disruption of the splice site, resulting in shortened protein product; however, the reading frame remained intact. Based on these 2 features, the SV was downgraded as a variant of undetermined significance. Due to inconclusive evidence that the specific SV was pathogenic, pregnancy termination was not recommended (choice D). Pregnancy termination is a multifaceted subject with psychosocial, cultural, and medical implications, differing across communities worldwide and beyond the scope of this discussion. Following a multidisciplinary evaluation, the fetus was not delivered prematurely, noting associated risks of early fetal delivery, lack of radiological evidence of intraocular tumors, and further genetic evaluation downgrading pathogenicity of the incidental variant (choice A). Routine prenatal observation without additional investigations for suspicious intraocular pathologies may not be sufficient to rule out retinoblastoma and was therefore performed in collaboration with clinical geneticists and multimodal fetal imaging (choice B). Follow-up fetal magnetic resonance imaging performed at 38 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any intraocular tumors or intracranial abnormalities suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma. The parents decided to continue the pregnancy. The child was born at 39 weeks and 6 days without complications. Examination demonstrated no evidence of intraocular tumors but was not performed under anesthesia per the parents’ request. The child, currently aged 10 months, continues to be evaluated periodically to rule out retinoblastoma, and is currently without any pathogenic ocular abnormalities.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: RB1pathogenic sequence variant in a 29-week-old fetus with no family history or sonographic features suggestive of retinoblastoma. C. Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents Retinoblastoma, with an incidence of 1 in 17 000 live births, is typically diagnosed within a few years of life.2Early treatment can lead to nearly 100% survival rate. Prognosis is poor with delayed diagnosis or treatment.2Inherited retinoblastoma occurs at a younger age than sporadic disease, tends to be bilateral,3and results from biallelic pathogenic SVs (PSVs) in theRB1gene in a precursor retinal cell.4,5An inherited mutated allele (ie, germline PSV) predisposes to tumorigenesis in utero or after birth in 40% of retinoblastoma cases, with high penetrance of the disease.3,5,6 Current evidence suggests screening at-risk newborns (ie, those with a family history of retinoblastoma) until 4 years of age.7Prenatal molecular screening facilitates earlier detection, potentially improving family planning, genetic counseling, and earlier interventions.4,8For example, planned delivery for prenatally confirmed carriers ofRB1mutations can lead to earlier diagnosis, reduced treatment-associated morbidity, and favorable visual outcomes.4However, early fetal delivery has potential risks, including physical and neurocognitive delay, warranting cautious evaluation by multidisciplinary teams.4,8Furthermore, while no threshold exists for planned early delivery, premature delivery may be achieved effectively with active intervention following 26 weeks’ gestation.9 InactivatingRB1germline PSVs have been associated with high penetrance, with most PSV carriers developing intraocular tumors by early childhood. However, phenotypic presentation may differ among individuals, even among identical PSV carriers.3,6Alekseeva et al6reported a substantial prevalence of asymptomatic mutatedRB1PSV carriers among parents of retinoblastoma patients with more children inheriting a defectiveRB1gene from the father, suggesting parental origin may affect retinoblastoma penetrance. In another study, individuals harboring low-penetranceRB1PSVs (eg, splice-site and missense SVs) developed bilateral retinoblastoma later than patients with null PSVs.4Molecular screening methods (eg, RNA sequencing of amniotic fluid cells) have enabled clinicians to assess whether a specificRB1SV is likely to be associated with any phenotypic manifestations.10However, there currently are no clinically acceptable predictive parameters to better define the phenotypic expression ofRB1PSV carriers. The case presented herein reports an incidentalRB1PSV detected on unrelated genetic testing, posing a clinical and ethical dilemma to both clinician and family.3,4,6,8 Both parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (choice C), confirming the father, with no history of cancer, harbored the same genetic SV as the fetus, decreasing the possibility that the SV was pathogenic. RNA sequencing demonstrated disruption of the splice site, resulting in shortened protein product; however, the reading frame remained intact. Based on these 2 features, the SV was downgraded as a variant of undetermined significance. Due to inconclusive evidence that the specific SV was pathogenic, pregnancy termination was not recommended (choice D). Pregnancy termination is a multifaceted subject with psychosocial, cultural, and medical implications, differing across communities worldwide and beyond the scope of this discussion. Following a multidisciplinary evaluation, the fetus was not delivered prematurely, noting associated risks of early fetal delivery, lack of radiological evidence of intraocular tumors, and further genetic evaluation downgrading pathogenicity of the incidental variant (choice A). Routine prenatal observation without additional investigations for suspicious intraocular pathologies may not be sufficient to rule out retinoblastoma and was therefore performed in collaboration with clinical geneticists and multimodal fetal imaging (choice B). Follow-up fetal magnetic resonance imaging performed at 38 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any intraocular tumors or intracranial abnormalities suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma. The parents decided to continue the pregnancy. The child was born at 39 weeks and 6 days without complications. Examination demonstrated no evidence of intraocular tumors but was not performed under anesthesia per the parents’ request. The child, currently aged 10 months, continues to be evaluated periodically to rule out retinoblastoma, and is currently without any pathogenic ocular abnormalities.

This specificRB1SV had not been previously reported in any genetic databases, but was deemed pathogenic by Invitae, the commercial laboratory, in line with the American College of Medical Genetics and their guidelines for interpretation of sequence variants.1No intraocular tumors were found on fetal sonography. There was no discernable family history of retinoblastoma or ocular disorders, and complete ophthalmic evaluation of both parents was normal with no suspected retinomas.

options.C: Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents

case_info.answer: Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents
case_info.explanation: RB1pathogenic sequence variant in a 29-week-old fetus with no family history or sonographic features suggestive of retinoblastoma. C. Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents Retinoblastoma, with an incidence of 1 in 17 000 live births, is typically diagnosed within a few years of life.2Early treatment can lead to nearly 100% survival rate. Prognosis is poor with delayed diagnosis or treatment.2Inherited retinoblastoma occurs at a younger age than sporadic disease, tends to be bilateral,3and results from biallelic pathogenic SVs (PSVs) in theRB1gene in a precursor retinal cell.4,5An inherited mutated allele (ie, germline PSV) predisposes to tumorigenesis in utero or after birth in 40% of retinoblastoma cases, with high penetrance of the disease.3,5,6 Current evidence suggests screening at-risk newborns (ie, those with a family history of retinoblastoma) until 4 years of age.7Prenatal molecular screening facilitates earlier detection, potentially improving family planning, genetic counseling, and earlier interventions.4,8For example, planned delivery for prenatally confirmed carriers ofRB1mutations can lead to earlier diagnosis, reduced treatment-associated morbidity, and favorable visual outcomes.4However, early fetal delivery has potential risks, including physical and neurocognitive delay, warranting cautious evaluation by multidisciplinary teams.4,8Furthermore, while no threshold exists for planned early delivery, premature delivery may be achieved effectively with active intervention following 26 weeks’ gestation.9 InactivatingRB1germline PSVs have been associated with high penetrance, with most PSV carriers developing intraocular tumors by early childhood. However, phenotypic presentation may differ among individuals, even among identical PSV carriers.3,6Alekseeva et al6reported a substantial prevalence of asymptomatic mutatedRB1PSV carriers among parents of retinoblastoma patients with more children inheriting a defectiveRB1gene from the father, suggesting parental origin may affect retinoblastoma penetrance. In another study, individuals harboring low-penetranceRB1PSVs (eg, splice-site and missense SVs) developed bilateral retinoblastoma later than patients with null PSVs.4Molecular screening methods (eg, RNA sequencing of amniotic fluid cells) have enabled clinicians to assess whether a specificRB1SV is likely to be associated with any phenotypic manifestations.10However, there currently are no clinically acceptable predictive parameters to better define the phenotypic expression ofRB1PSV carriers. The case presented herein reports an incidentalRB1PSV detected on unrelated genetic testing, posing a clinical and ethical dilemma to both clinician and family.3,4,6,8 Both parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (choice C), confirming the father, with no history of cancer, harbored the same genetic SV as the fetus, decreasing the possibility that the SV was pathogenic. RNA sequencing demonstrated disruption of the splice site, resulting in shortened protein product; however, the reading frame remained intact. Based on these 2 features, the SV was downgraded as a variant of undetermined significance. Due to inconclusive evidence that the specific SV was pathogenic, pregnancy termination was not recommended (choice D). Pregnancy termination is a multifaceted subject with psychosocial, cultural, and medical implications, differing across communities worldwide and beyond the scope of this discussion. Following a multidisciplinary evaluation, the fetus was not delivered prematurely, noting associated risks of early fetal delivery, lack of radiological evidence of intraocular tumors, and further genetic evaluation downgrading pathogenicity of the incidental variant (choice A). Routine prenatal observation without additional investigations for suspicious intraocular pathologies may not be sufficient to rule out retinoblastoma and was therefore performed in collaboration with clinical geneticists and multimodal fetal imaging (choice B). Follow-up fetal magnetic resonance imaging performed at 38 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any intraocular tumors or intracranial abnormalities suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma. The parents decided to continue the pregnancy. The child was born at 39 weeks and 6 days without complications. Examination demonstrated no evidence of intraocular tumors but was not performed under anesthesia per the parents’ request. The child, currently aged 10 months, continues to be evaluated periodically to rule out retinoblastoma, and is currently without any pathogenic ocular abnormalities.

1 = Very low workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: RB1pathogenic sequence variant in a 29-week-old fetus with no family history or sonographic features suggestive of retinoblastoma. C. Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents Retinoblastoma, with an incidence of 1 in 17 000 live births, is typically diagnosed within a few years of life.2Early treatment can lead to nearly 100% survival rate. Prognosis is poor with delayed diagnosis or treatment.2Inherited retinoblastoma occurs at a younger age than sporadic disease, tends to be bilateral,3and results from biallelic pathogenic SVs (PSVs) in theRB1gene in a precursor retinal cell.4,5An inherited mutated allele (ie, germline PSV) predisposes to tumorigenesis in utero or after birth in 40% of retinoblastoma cases, with high penetrance of the disease.3,5,6 Current evidence suggests screening at-risk newborns (ie, those with a family history of retinoblastoma) until 4 years of age.7Prenatal molecular screening facilitates earlier detection, potentially improving family planning, genetic counseling, and earlier interventions.4,8For example, planned delivery for prenatally confirmed carriers ofRB1mutations can lead to earlier diagnosis, reduced treatment-associated morbidity, and favorable visual outcomes.4However, early fetal delivery has potential risks, including physical and neurocognitive delay, warranting cautious evaluation by multidisciplinary teams.4,8Furthermore, while no threshold exists for planned early delivery, premature delivery may be achieved effectively with active intervention following 26 weeks’ gestation.9 InactivatingRB1germline PSVs have been associated with high penetrance, with most PSV carriers developing intraocular tumors by early childhood. However, phenotypic presentation may differ among individuals, even among identical PSV carriers.3,6Alekseeva et al6reported a substantial prevalence of asymptomatic mutatedRB1PSV carriers among parents of retinoblastoma patients with more children inheriting a defectiveRB1gene from the father, suggesting parental origin may affect retinoblastoma penetrance. In another study, individuals harboring low-penetranceRB1PSVs (eg, splice-site and missense SVs) developed bilateral retinoblastoma later than patients with null PSVs.4Molecular screening methods (eg, RNA sequencing of amniotic fluid cells) have enabled clinicians to assess whether a specificRB1SV is likely to be associated with any phenotypic manifestations.10However, there currently are no clinically acceptable predictive parameters to better define the phenotypic expression ofRB1PSV carriers. The case presented herein reports an incidentalRB1PSV detected on unrelated genetic testing, posing a clinical and ethical dilemma to both clinician and family.3,4,6,8 Both parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (choice C), confirming the father, with no history of cancer, harbored the same genetic SV as the fetus, decreasing the possibility that the SV was pathogenic. RNA sequencing demonstrated disruption of the splice site, resulting in shortened protein product; however, the reading frame remained intact. Based on these 2 features, the SV was downgraded as a variant of undetermined significance. Due to inconclusive evidence that the specific SV was pathogenic, pregnancy termination was not recommended (choice D). Pregnancy termination is a multifaceted subject with psychosocial, cultural, and medical implications, differing across communities worldwide and beyond the scope of this discussion. Following a multidisciplinary evaluation, the fetus was not delivered prematurely, noting associated risks of early fetal delivery, lack of radiological evidence of intraocular tumors, and further genetic evaluation downgrading pathogenicity of the incidental variant (choice A). Routine prenatal observation without additional investigations for suspicious intraocular pathologies may not be sufficient to rule out retinoblastoma and was therefore performed in collaboration with clinical geneticists and multimodal fetal imaging (choice B). Follow-up fetal magnetic resonance imaging performed at 38 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any intraocular tumors or intracranial abnormalities suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma. The parents decided to continue the pregnancy. The child was born at 39 weeks and 6 days without complications. Examination demonstrated no evidence of intraocular tumors but was not performed under anesthesia per the parents’ request. The child, currently aged 10 months, continues to be evaluated periodically to rule out retinoblastoma, and is currently without any pathogenic ocular abnormalities.

case_info.explanation: RB1pathogenic sequence variant in a 29-week-old fetus with no family history or sonographic features suggestive of retinoblastoma. C. Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents Retinoblastoma, with an incidence of 1 in 17 000 live births, is typically diagnosed within a few years of life.2Early treatment can lead to nearly 100% survival rate. Prognosis is poor with delayed diagnosis or treatment.2Inherited retinoblastoma occurs at a younger age than sporadic disease, tends to be bilateral,3and results from biallelic pathogenic SVs (PSVs) in theRB1gene in a precursor retinal cell.4,5An inherited mutated allele (ie, germline PSV) predisposes to tumorigenesis in utero or after birth in 40% of retinoblastoma cases, with high penetrance of the disease.3,5,6 Current evidence suggests screening at-risk newborns (ie, those with a family history of retinoblastoma) until 4 years of age.7Prenatal molecular screening facilitates earlier detection, potentially improving family planning, genetic counseling, and earlier interventions.4,8For example, planned delivery for prenatally confirmed carriers ofRB1mutations can lead to earlier diagnosis, reduced treatment-associated morbidity, and favorable visual outcomes.4However, early fetal delivery has potential risks, including physical and neurocognitive delay, warranting cautious evaluation by multidisciplinary teams.4,8Furthermore, while no threshold exists for planned early delivery, premature delivery may be achieved effectively with active intervention following 26 weeks’ gestation.9 InactivatingRB1germline PSVs have been associated with high penetrance, with most PSV carriers developing intraocular tumors by early childhood. However, phenotypic presentation may differ among individuals, even among identical PSV carriers.3,6Alekseeva et al6reported a substantial prevalence of asymptomatic mutatedRB1PSV carriers among parents of retinoblastoma patients with more children inheriting a defectiveRB1gene from the father, suggesting parental origin may affect retinoblastoma penetrance. In another study, individuals harboring low-penetranceRB1PSVs (eg, splice-site and missense SVs) developed bilateral retinoblastoma later than patients with null PSVs.4Molecular screening methods (eg, RNA sequencing of amniotic fluid cells) have enabled clinicians to assess whether a specificRB1SV is likely to be associated with any phenotypic manifestations.10However, there currently are no clinically acceptable predictive parameters to better define the phenotypic expression ofRB1PSV carriers. The case presented herein reports an incidentalRB1PSV detected on unrelated genetic testing, posing a clinical and ethical dilemma to both clinician and family.3,4,6,8 Both parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (choice C), confirming the father, with no history of cancer, harbored the same genetic SV as the fetus, decreasing the possibility that the SV was pathogenic. RNA sequencing demonstrated disruption of the splice site, resulting in shortened protein product; however, the reading frame remained intact. Based on these 2 features, the SV was downgraded as a variant of undetermined significance. Due to inconclusive evidence that the specific SV was pathogenic, pregnancy termination was not recommended (choice D). Pregnancy termination is a multifaceted subject with psychosocial, cultural, and medical implications, differing across communities worldwide and beyond the scope of this discussion. Following a multidisciplinary evaluation, the fetus was not delivered prematurely, noting associated risks of early fetal delivery, lack of radiological evidence of intraocular tumors, and further genetic evaluation downgrading pathogenicity of the incidental variant (choice A). Routine prenatal observation without additional investigations for suspicious intraocular pathologies may not be sufficient to rule out retinoblastoma and was therefore performed in collaboration with clinical geneticists and multimodal fetal imaging (choice B). Follow-up fetal magnetic resonance imaging performed at 38 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any intraocular tumors or intracranial abnormalities suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma. The parents decided to continue the pregnancy. The child was born at 39 weeks and 6 days without complications. Examination demonstrated no evidence of intraocular tumors but was not performed under anesthesia per the parents’ request. The child, currently aged 10 months, continues to be evaluated periodically to rule out retinoblastoma, and is currently without any pathogenic ocular abnormalities.

1. Mental Demand

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration

   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.explanation: RB1pathogenic sequence variant in a 29-week-old fetus with no family history or sonographic features suggestive of retinoblastoma. C. Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents Retinoblastoma, with an incidence of 1 in 17 000 live births, is typically diagnosed within a few years of life.2Early treatment can lead to nearly 100% survival rate. Prognosis is poor with delayed diagnosis or treatment.2Inherited retinoblastoma occurs at a younger age than sporadic disease, tends to be bilateral,3and results from biallelic pathogenic SVs (PSVs) in theRB1gene in a precursor retinal cell.4,5An inherited mutated allele (ie, germline PSV) predisposes to tumorigenesis in utero or after birth in 40% of retinoblastoma cases, with high penetrance of the disease.3,5,6 Current evidence suggests screening at-risk newborns (ie, those with a family history of retinoblastoma) until 4 years of age.7Prenatal molecular screening facilitates earlier detection, potentially improving family planning, genetic counseling, and earlier interventions.4,8For example, planned delivery for prenatally confirmed carriers ofRB1mutations can lead to earlier diagnosis, reduced treatment-associated morbidity, and favorable visual outcomes.4However, early fetal delivery has potential risks, including physical and neurocognitive delay, warranting cautious evaluation by multidisciplinary teams.4,8Furthermore, while no threshold exists for planned early delivery, premature delivery may be achieved effectively with active intervention following 26 weeks’ gestation.9 InactivatingRB1germline PSVs have been associated with high penetrance, with most PSV carriers developing intraocular tumors by early childhood. However, phenotypic presentation may differ among individuals, even among identical PSV carriers.3,6Alekseeva et al6reported a substantial prevalence of asymptomatic mutatedRB1PSV carriers among parents of retinoblastoma patients with more children inheriting a defectiveRB1gene from the father, suggesting parental origin may affect retinoblastoma penetrance. In another study, individuals harboring low-penetranceRB1PSVs (eg, splice-site and missense SVs) developed bilateral retinoblastoma later than patients with null PSVs.4Molecular screening methods (eg, RNA sequencing of amniotic fluid cells) have enabled clinicians to assess whether a specificRB1SV is likely to be associated with any phenotypic manifestations.10However, there currently are no clinically acceptable predictive parameters to better define the phenotypic expression ofRB1PSV carriers. The case presented herein reports an incidentalRB1PSV detected on unrelated genetic testing, posing a clinical and ethical dilemma to both clinician and family.3,4,6,8 Both parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (choice C), confirming the father, with no history of cancer, harbored the same genetic SV as the fetus, decreasing the possibility that the SV was pathogenic. RNA sequencing demonstrated disruption of the splice site, resulting in shortened protein product; however, the reading frame remained intact. Based on these 2 features, the SV was downgraded as a variant of undetermined significance. Due to inconclusive evidence that the specific SV was pathogenic, pregnancy termination was not recommended (choice D). Pregnancy termination is a multifaceted subject with psychosocial, cultural, and medical implications, differing across communities worldwide and beyond the scope of this discussion. Following a multidisciplinary evaluation, the fetus was not delivered prematurely, noting associated risks of early fetal delivery, lack of radiological evidence of intraocular tumors, and further genetic evaluation downgrading pathogenicity of the incidental variant (choice A). Routine prenatal observation without additional investigations for suspicious intraocular pathologies may not be sufficient to rule out retinoblastoma and was therefore performed in collaboration with clinical geneticists and multimodal fetal imaging (choice B). Follow-up fetal magnetic resonance imaging performed at 38 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any intraocular tumors or intracranial abnormalities suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma. The parents decided to continue the pregnancy. The child was born at 39 weeks and 6 days without complications. Examination demonstrated no evidence of intraocular tumors but was not performed under anesthesia per the parents’ request. The child, currently aged 10 months, continues to be evaluated periodically to rule out retinoblastoma, and is currently without any pathogenic ocular abnormalities.

case_info.explanation: RB1pathogenic sequence variant in a 29-week-old fetus with no family history or sonographic features suggestive of retinoblastoma. C. Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents Retinoblastoma, with an incidence of 1 in 17 000 live births, is typically diagnosed within a few years of life.2Early treatment can lead to nearly 100% survival rate. Prognosis is poor with delayed diagnosis or treatment.2Inherited retinoblastoma occurs at a younger age than sporadic disease, tends to be bilateral,3and results from biallelic pathogenic SVs (PSVs) in theRB1gene in a precursor retinal cell.4,5An inherited mutated allele (ie, germline PSV) predisposes to tumorigenesis in utero or after birth in 40% of retinoblastoma cases, with high penetrance of the disease.3,5,6 Current evidence suggests screening at-risk newborns (ie, those with a family history of retinoblastoma) until 4 years of age.7Prenatal molecular screening facilitates earlier detection, potentially improving family planning, genetic counseling, and earlier interventions.4,8For example, planned delivery for prenatally confirmed carriers ofRB1mutations can lead to earlier diagnosis, reduced treatment-associated morbidity, and favorable visual outcomes.4However, early fetal delivery has potential risks, including physical and neurocognitive delay, warranting cautious evaluation by multidisciplinary teams.4,8Furthermore, while no threshold exists for planned early delivery, premature delivery may be achieved effectively with active intervention following 26 weeks’ gestation.9 InactivatingRB1germline PSVs have been associated with high penetrance, with most PSV carriers developing intraocular tumors by early childhood. However, phenotypic presentation may differ among individuals, even among identical PSV carriers.3,6Alekseeva et al6reported a substantial prevalence of asymptomatic mutatedRB1PSV carriers among parents of retinoblastoma patients with more children inheriting a defectiveRB1gene from the father, suggesting parental origin may affect retinoblastoma penetrance. In another study, individuals harboring low-penetranceRB1PSVs (eg, splice-site and missense SVs) developed bilateral retinoblastoma later than patients with null PSVs.4Molecular screening methods (eg, RNA sequencing of amniotic fluid cells) have enabled clinicians to assess whether a specificRB1SV is likely to be associated with any phenotypic manifestations.10However, there currently are no clinically acceptable predictive parameters to better define the phenotypic expression ofRB1PSV carriers. The case presented herein reports an incidentalRB1PSV detected on unrelated genetic testing, posing a clinical and ethical dilemma to both clinician and family.3,4,6,8 Both parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (choice C), confirming the father, with no history of cancer, harbored the same genetic SV as the fetus, decreasing the possibility that the SV was pathogenic. RNA sequencing demonstrated disruption of the splice site, resulting in shortened protein product; however, the reading frame remained intact. Based on these 2 features, the SV was downgraded as a variant of undetermined significance. Due to inconclusive evidence that the specific SV was pathogenic, pregnancy termination was not recommended (choice D). Pregnancy termination is a multifaceted subject with psychosocial, cultural, and medical implications, differing across communities worldwide and beyond the scope of this discussion. Following a multidisciplinary evaluation, the fetus was not delivered prematurely, noting associated risks of early fetal delivery, lack of radiological evidence of intraocular tumors, and further genetic evaluation downgrading pathogenicity of the incidental variant (choice A). Routine prenatal observation without additional investigations for suspicious intraocular pathologies may not be sufficient to rule out retinoblastoma and was therefore performed in collaboration with clinical geneticists and multimodal fetal imaging (choice B). Follow-up fetal magnetic resonance imaging performed at 38 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any intraocular tumors or intracranial abnormalities suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma. The parents decided to continue the pregnancy. The child was born at 39 weeks and 6 days without complications. Examination demonstrated no evidence of intraocular tumors but was not performed under anesthesia per the parents’ request. The child, currently aged 10 months, continues to be evaluated periodically to rule out retinoblastoma, and is currently without any pathogenic ocular abnormalities.

1. Mental Demand

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

case_info.explanation: RB1pathogenic sequence variant in a 29-week-old fetus with no family history or sonographic features suggestive of retinoblastoma. C. Further genetic evaluation of the fetus and parents Retinoblastoma, with an incidence of 1 in 17 000 live births, is typically diagnosed within a few years of life.2Early treatment can lead to nearly 100% survival rate. Prognosis is poor with delayed diagnosis or treatment.2Inherited retinoblastoma occurs at a younger age than sporadic disease, tends to be bilateral,3and results from biallelic pathogenic SVs (PSVs) in theRB1gene in a precursor retinal cell.4,5An inherited mutated allele (ie, germline PSV) predisposes to tumorigenesis in utero or after birth in 40% of retinoblastoma cases, with high penetrance of the disease.3,5,6 Current evidence suggests screening at-risk newborns (ie, those with a family history of retinoblastoma) until 4 years of age.7Prenatal molecular screening facilitates earlier detection, potentially improving family planning, genetic counseling, and earlier interventions.4,8For example, planned delivery for prenatally confirmed carriers ofRB1mutations can lead to earlier diagnosis, reduced treatment-associated morbidity, and favorable visual outcomes.4However, early fetal delivery has potential risks, including physical and neurocognitive delay, warranting cautious evaluation by multidisciplinary teams.4,8Furthermore, while no threshold exists for planned early delivery, premature delivery may be achieved effectively with active intervention following 26 weeks’ gestation.9 InactivatingRB1germline PSVs have been associated with high penetrance, with most PSV carriers developing intraocular tumors by early childhood. However, phenotypic presentation may differ among individuals, even among identical PSV carriers.3,6Alekseeva et al6reported a substantial prevalence of asymptomatic mutatedRB1PSV carriers among parents of retinoblastoma patients with more children inheriting a defectiveRB1gene from the father, suggesting parental origin may affect retinoblastoma penetrance. In another study, individuals harboring low-penetranceRB1PSVs (eg, splice-site and missense SVs) developed bilateral retinoblastoma later than patients with null PSVs.4Molecular screening methods (eg, RNA sequencing of amniotic fluid cells) have enabled clinicians to assess whether a specificRB1SV is likely to be associated with any phenotypic manifestations.10However, there currently are no clinically acceptable predictive parameters to better define the phenotypic expression ofRB1PSV carriers. The case presented herein reports an incidentalRB1PSV detected on unrelated genetic testing, posing a clinical and ethical dilemma to both clinician and family.3,4,6,8 Both parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (choice C), confirming the father, with no history of cancer, harbored the same genetic SV as the fetus, decreasing the possibility that the SV was pathogenic. RNA sequencing demonstrated disruption of the splice site, resulting in shortened protein product; however, the reading frame remained intact. Based on these 2 features, the SV was downgraded as a variant of undetermined significance. Due to inconclusive evidence that the specific SV was pathogenic, pregnancy termination was not recommended (choice D). Pregnancy termination is a multifaceted subject with psychosocial, cultural, and medical implications, differing across communities worldwide and beyond the scope of this discussion. Following a multidisciplinary evaluation, the fetus was not delivered prematurely, noting associated risks of early fetal delivery, lack of radiological evidence of intraocular tumors, and further genetic evaluation downgrading pathogenicity of the incidental variant (choice A). Routine prenatal observation without additional investigations for suspicious intraocular pathologies may not be sufficient to rule out retinoblastoma and was therefore performed in collaboration with clinical geneticists and multimodal fetal imaging (choice B). Follow-up fetal magnetic resonance imaging performed at 38 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any intraocular tumors or intracranial abnormalities suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma. The parents decided to continue the pregnancy. The child was born at 39 weeks and 6 days without complications. Examination demonstrated no evidence of intraocular tumors but was not performed under anesthesia per the parents’ request. The child, currently aged 10 months, continues to be evaluated periodically to rule out retinoblastoma, and is currently without any pathogenic ocular abnormalities.
